concepts.def: The UK population is growing and ageing, driven by natural change and migration, increasing demand for housing, services and infrastructure.
Demand for homes outstrips supply, especially in south-east England, raising prices and forcing difficult decisions about where to build.
Greenfield sites are undeveloped land, often on city edges, while brownfield sites were previously built on; each has costs and benefits for housing.
Land around cities protected from most development to limit urban sprawl, though it constrains where new homes can be built.
The combination of fossil fuels, nuclear and growing renewables used to supply the UK's energy, shifting over time to cut carbon emissions.
The UK aims to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through renewable energy, efficiency, transport changes and its legally binding net zero target.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Geographical Investigations: UK Challenges — a core area of GCSE Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Geographical Investigations: UK Challenges brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Geographical Investigations: UK Challenges.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: The UK's legally binding net zero emissions target year is:
Green belt policy is designed to:
options: Prevent urban sprawl by restricting development around cities
Increase parking in city centres
Encourage out-of-town shopping centres
Protect beaches from erosion

mcqs.q: Which trend increases pressure on UK housing supply?
options: A rising population and more single-person households
A rapidly falling population
Shrinking demand for homes in the south-east
Declining household formation everywhere

mcqs.q: Is building on brownfield sites always better than greenfield?
options: Brownfield development has no drawbacks.
Brownfield sites are fields where brown crops are grown.
Not always — brownfield reuses urban land and existing services, but sites can be costly to decontaminate and too small, so some greenfield building may still be needed.
Renewable energy only works in the summer months.

mcqs.q: Does the green belt stop all building around cities?
options: No — it strongly restricts development, but exceptions exist and land can be released; it can also push development beyond the belt, lengthening commutes.
Renewable energy only works in the summer months.
The green belt is a ring road painted green.
Green belt land can never be built on.

mcqs.q: Could the UK switch entirely to wind and solar power today?
options: The UK could run on 100% wind and solar tomorrow without problems.
The green belt is a ring road painted green.
Renewable energy only works in the summer months.
Not yet — wind and solar are intermittent, so the energy mix still needs storage, nuclear or gas backup while grid and battery technology develop.

Use sampling (random/systematic) to gather data in the field
